steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Latin word order is much freer than English because grammatical relationships are shown by case endings, not position. The most common order is Subject-Object-Verb (SOV).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The verb typically comes at or near the end of a Latin sentence, which is the biggest difference from English SVO order.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Adjectives must agree with the noun they modify in gender, number, and case (GNC): puella bona (good girl, fem. nom. sg.), servum bonum (good slave, masc. acc. sg.).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Relative clauses use the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod (who, which, that) which must agree with its antecedent in gender and number, but takes its case from its own clause.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the typical word order of a Latin sentence? | Q: What does GNC agreement mean for adjectives? | Q: How does the relative pronoun agree with its antecedent?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Subject-Object-Verb (SOV). The verb usually comes at or near the end. However, word order is flexible because case endings show grammatical relationships. | Gender, Number, Case: an adjective must match the noun it describes in all three. For example, puella bona (fem. nom. sg.) but servum bonum (masc. acc. sg.). | The relative pronoun agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case is determined by its function within the relative clause itself.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always identify the main verb first when translating — it anchors the sentence and tells you the tense and subject. For relative pronouns, find the antecedent first (match gender and number), then work out the pronoun's case from its clause. Accusative + infinitive is tested in every exam: look for a verb of saying/thinking/knowing followed by accusative noun + infinitive. When you see ut + subjunctive, check the main clause for tam/tantus/ita to decide if it is purpose or result.
